```{r}
#| include: false
# The preamble every chapter needs, in one place.
#
# Each chapter renders in a session of its own, so each one has to attach the
# package, point reticulate at the book's virtualenv, and hold the tables the
# examples run on. Written once here and pulled in with
# `{{< include ../_setup.qmd >}}` at the top of every chapter.
#
# **The leading underscore is not decoration.** All three book tools skip any
# path containing `/_`, so this file is not scanned for prose and is not mistaken
# for a chapter. It carries no prose to scan.
# **Paths are found by walking up rather than counted from here.** A chapter in
# `book/chapters/` and a page at `book/` are different distances from the
# package, and knitr runs each chunk from its own file's directory, so a fixed
# `../` is right for exactly one of them. Walking up is what both packages
# already do to find `god-cli`, and it does not care how deep a chapter sits.
find_up <- function(target) {
  directory <- normalizePath(getwd())
  repeat {
    candidate <- file.path(directory, target)
    if (file.exists(candidate)) return(candidate)
    parent <- dirname(directory)
    if (identical(parent, directory)) stop("cannot find ", target, " above ", getwd())
    directory <- parent
  }
}

suppressMessages(
  pkgload::load_all(find_up("r-pkg/god"), export_all = FALSE, quiet = TRUE)
)
options(width = 76)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
# **Its own chunk, so a missing virtualenv cannot take the tables with it.**
# Rendering needs this: every chapter's Python tab is reached through
# reticulate. The book's guards do not, because they read and evaluate the R
# chunks only.
#
# Sharing one chunk with the fixtures meant that anywhere `book/.venv` is absent
# the preamble stopped on this line and every table below went undefined. The CI
# job that has no virtualenv reported that as *one* broken chunk rather than
# twenty, because the R suite's own `sales` was sitting in the global
# environment and stood in for the book's wherever a chapter asked for it. Only
# `marks` had no understudy. A guard passing on the wrong table is worse than
# one failing, and it took a red job on a fresh machine to see it.
library(reticulate)
use_virtualenv(find_up("book/.venv"), required = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
# The engine announces where it keeps its extensions the first time anything
# connects to it. Spending that first connection here means the announcement
# lands in a hidden chunk rather than in the middle of a reader's first example.
invisible(capture.output(
  suppressMessages(collect(data.frame(a = 1) |> take(1)))
))

# **The cast is declared in the preface, and its shapes are load-bearing for
# chapters, so change a value here only with the blast radius in mind: every
# rendered table in the book is computed from these rows.** sales is built so
# grouped answers are checkable by eye: each product's unit price and unit
# cost are constant (Widget 25/10, Gadget 60/40, Doohickey 40/25, Sprocket
# 15/12), so revenue and cost are exact multiples of quantity everywhere.
# Three regions, four products, a year of dates crossing a year boundary,
# revenue ties at 120, 150 and 200 for the chapters on rank, and no Sprocket
# in the North, for the chapters on what is missing. Dates stay ISO text in
# both languages: a real R Date against a pandas datetime64 prints
# differently, and ISO text sorts correctly as it is.
sales <- data.frame(
  date     = c("2025-11-03", "2025-11-17", "2025-12-05", "2025-12-22",
               "2026-01-09", "2026-01-26", "2026-02-14", "2026-03-03",
               "2026-04-11", "2026-05-06", "2026-06-19", "2026-07-08",
               "2026-08-24", "2026-09-15", "2026-10-02"),
  region   = c("West", "East", "West", "North", "East", "West", "North",
               "East", "West", "North", "East", "West", "North", "East",
               "West"),
  product  = c("Widget", "Gadget", "Doohickey", "Widget", "Widget", "Gadget",
               "Doohickey", "Doohickey", "Widget", "Gadget", "Sprocket",
               "Sprocket", "Widget", "Gadget", "Widget"),
  quantity = c(4L, 2L, 3L, 6L, 8L, 5L, 2L, 5L, 2L, 4L, 10L, 6L, 3L, 1L, 5L),
  revenue  = c(100, 120, 120, 150, 200, 300, 80, 200, 50, 240, 150, 90, 75,
               60, 125),
  cost     = c(40, 80, 75, 60, 80, 200, 50, 125, 20, 160, 120, 72, 30, 40,
               50),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Mismatched with sales in both directions, on purpose: sales has Sprocket
# rows and products has no Sprocket, products has Gizmo and sales sold none.
# An inner join loses quietly in one direction and an unmatched row waits in
# the other, which is what the joining chapters exist to show.
products <- data.frame(
  product = c("Widget", "Gadget", "Doohickey", "Gizmo"),
  maker   = c("Acme", "Globex", "Initech", "Initrode"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# The three tables that more than one chapter needs. Each is also defined
# visibly in the chapter that introduces it, because a reader meeting a table
# should see what is in it. This copy is what keeps a *later* chapter working.
# Wide on purpose: eight score columns are what selecting by the shape of a
# name is for, and a chapter arguing against naming columns by hand needs a
# table where doing so would actually hurt.
survey <- data.frame(
  respondent = 1:6,
  name       = c("ana", "ben", "cal", "dee", "eli", "fay"),
  region     = c("West", "East", "North", "West", "East", "North"),
  joined     = c("2026-01-12", "2026-02-03", "2026-02-27", "2026-03-15",
                 "2026-04-01", "2026-04-22"),
  q1_score   = c(4L, 5L, 3L, 4L, 2L, 5L),
  q2_score   = c(2L, 5L, 5L, 3L, 4L, 4L),
  q3_score   = c(5L, 4L, 2L, 5L, 3L, 4L),
  q4_score   = c(3L, 3L, 4L, 2L, 5L, 5L),
  q5_score   = c(4L, 2L, 5L, 4L, 4L, 3L),
  q6_score   = c(5L, 5L, 3L, 3L, 2L, 4L),
  q7_score   = c(2L, 4L, 4L, 5L, 3L, 5L),
  q8_score   = c(3L, 5L, 2L, 4L, 5L, 4L),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

answers <- data.frame(
  student = c("ann", "bob"),
  q1 = c(1, 4), q2 = c(2, 5), q3 = c(3, 6),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

marks <- data.frame(
  student  = c("ann", "ann", "bob", "bob"),
  question = c("q1", "q2", "q1", "q2"),
  mark     = c(1, 2, 4, 5),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# These two are introduced in one chapter and used again in the next, because
# the chapters they belong to were one long section before the book was split.
# `n` is written `7L` rather than `7` so R holds a whole number where Python
# does: a double there makes `to_text` say "7.0" in one language and "7" in the
# other, which is a fixture difference wearing a grammar difference's clothes.
messy <- data.frame(
  raw = c("  ann marie  ", "  bob  "),
  n = c(7L, 99L),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

diary <- data.frame(
  g = c("a", "a", "b"),
  on_ = c("2026-01-02", "2026-01-05", "2026-01-06"),
  x = c(10, 20, 30),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# The one table too large to check by eye, for the moments a verb has to
# prove it survives scale. 1,704 rows: Gapminder's country panel, CC BY 4.0,
# vendored beside the book so a render needs no network.
gapminder <- read.csv(find_up("book/data/gm_all.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
```

#| include: false
import sys, pathlib
# Walked up rather than counted, for the reason the R side gives above.
_here = pathlib.Path.cwd().resolve()
for _up in (_here, *_here.parents):

        sys.path.insert(0, str(_up / "py-pkg" / "god"))
        break
import pandas as pd
pd.set_option("display.width", 76)
from god import *

# The same fifteen rows as the R block above, in the same order, and they must
# stay identical or the two tabs of every example disagree for a reason that
# has nothing to do with the grammar. No missing cells in any integer column:
# pandas would promote the column to float and "4" would print as "4.0" in one
# language only.
sales = pd.DataFrame({
    "date":     ["2025-11-03", "2025-11-17", "2025-12-05", "2025-12-22",

                 "West"],
    "product":  ["Widget", "Gadget", "Doohickey", "Widget", "Widget",
                 "Gadget", "Doohickey", "Doohickey", "Widget", "Gadget",
                 "Sprocket", "Sprocket", "Widget", "Gadget", "Widget"],
    "quantity": [4, 2, 3, 6, 8, 5, 2, 5, 2, 4, 10, 6, 3, 1, 5],

                 75, 60, 125],

products = pd.DataFrame({

survey = pd.DataFrame({

                   "2026-04-01", "2026-04-22"],
